bivy.name: Thornton Lakes camp
bivy.water: The outlet of the lower lake, immediately at the sites.
bivy.capacity: Three individual sites, each capped at a party of four.
bivy.permit: A National Park Service wilderness permit is required. This is a designated camp rather than the Triumph cross-country zone, so it is a different reservation from the col — book the one you actually intend to sleep in. Bear canisters are required and campfires are not allowed; there is a composting toilet.
bivy.notes: Where the maintained trail ends, about five and a half miles in, at the outlet of the lower lake. It is the easy, legal, reliable option and the one to take if you arrive late or the col is booked out — but it leaves a very long summit day, since the col is still a thousand-plus feet of steep talus and grass above you. Most parties climbing the ridge push past it.

bivy.name: The Triumph col
bivy.water: Snowmelt — a small stream running off the snowpack, and pools near the sites; parties who want more drop toward the stream at the foot of the nearby snowfield. Every published description is of meltwater, and none says when it fails, so treat it as unreliable once the snow has gone.
bivy.capacity: Several good bivy spots on and just north of the col — nobody has had to drop to the glacier for want of ground. The real limit is the permit: the Triumph zone takes two parties a night, six people each.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit, in the Triumph cross-country zone: maximum party of six, and only two permits issued per night, which makes it one of the harder zones to get. It is one of the few zones that can be reserved in advance; roughly 40% of capacity is held back for walk-ups issued the day before or the day of, from the Wilderness Information Center at Marblemount. Cross-country camping is allowed only on durable ground — snow, rock or bare earth.
bivy.notes: The standard high camp, on the col northwest of the middle lake, gained by about 1,200 ft of steep talus and grass above the lakes — roughly seven and a half miles and 4,200 ft from the car. Flat ground, running water and a view straight into the Pickets. Published elevations disagree by about 150 ft, from roughly 5,750 to 5,900 ft, so do not plan an altitude-sensitive turnaround off a single figure. A rockier perch just below the col is also used and is well liked.

bivy.name: On-ridge bivy above the notch
bivy.water: None. Everything comes up from the col with you.
bivy.capacity: A couple of small platforms — a party of two or three, spread out.
bivy.notes: Small sites on the crest a hundred to two hundred feet above the notch, one or two pitches up the Northeast Ridge. Parties use them to shorten the climbing day, at the cost of carrying a full day's water onto the ridge. Several trip reports pass through them at dawn rather than sleep there, so treat the ground as confirmed and the comfort as unknown.

bivy.name: Meadow basin below the northwest-ridge saddle
bivy.water: Running water at the camp, fed by semi-permanent snowfields just above; those patches are described as holding meltwater well into the later part of the season.
bivy.capacity: No published tent count. The binding number is the permit: six people per party, six parties a night in the zone.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit, Bear Mountain cross-country zone: maximum party of six and six permits per night. This zone cannot be reserved in advance — it is walk-up only, from the Wilderness Information Center. Cross-country camping is restricted to durable ground.
bivy.notes: The standard and effectively the only high camp for the buttress, in heather meadow a little below the notch on the northwest ridge, where scattered trees give some wind shelter and flat grassy ground. Reached by climbing roughly 3,000 ft out of the Bear Creek valley to treeline on a rough climbers' path through open forest that gives way to blueberry brush. Around nine hours from the Chilliwack Lake road on the Canadian side; the American approach over Hannegan Pass and down the Chilliwack River is far longer, on the order of seventeen miles, but is the one that keeps the permit straightforward. Expect mosquitoes.

bivy.name: Saddle Lake
bivy.water: The lake — there is no running water here, and in a warm year it has been reported shrinking and buggy by mid-summer.
bivy.capacity: Not published. It is a small four-acre lake and the setback rule below pushes camps back off the water.
bivy.permit: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Boulder River Wilderness. Camping is prohibited within 200 ft slope distance of the shoreline of Saddle Lake and of Bandana Lake, and campfires are prohibited within the same 200 ft of both. No trailhead permit or quota is published for this trail, and the wilderness is closed throughout to pack and saddle stock.
bivy.notes: Two and a half miles in from Tupso Pass on a rough, root-bound forest trail — the first water and the first flat ground, but low and far from the mountain. Volunteers built a shelter at the meadow edge here in the early 1970s; no current source confirms it still stands or is usable, so do not plan on sleeping in it.

bivy.name: Goat Flats
bivy.water: Tarns only — there is no running water at the flats, and the tarn water has been described as stale by autumn. The last dependable running water is a stream well below, around the 4,200 ft mark; above the flats the next water is glacier and snow melt beyond Tin Can Gap. Late in a dry season, plan to carry from low down.
bivy.capacity: A number of established sites spread across the meadow, and it is regularly crowded on summer and autumn weekends. Camp only on ground that is already bare — the meadow is fragile and the Forest Service asks for existing sites only.
bivy.permit: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Boulder River Wilderness. Campfires are prohibited in the Goat Flats area outright, and also anywhere within a quarter mile of Trail 641 above Saddle Lake. No overnight permit or quota is published. There is a backcountry toilet at the flats; note that it must not be used for packed-out waste bags.
bivy.notes: The main camp for the peak, an open subalpine meadow on a ridge crest a little over two miles beyond Saddle Lake and roughly two and a half miles short of the lookout, with a view west to Puget Sound. Bears work the area, so bring a canister or another way to secure food. Published elevations for the flats come only from sources that could not be verified, so none is recorded here.

bivy.name: Tin Can Gap
bivy.water: Glacier and snow melt only.
bivy.capacity: A few spots at the gap and at the foot of the snow slope below it — small, and second choice to Goat Flats.
bivy.permit: The campfire closure along Trail 641 above Saddle Lake extends here.
bivy.notes: The last ground before the climbing starts: the Forest Service names it Tin Pan Gap, most climbers say Tin Can Gap, and it is where the route stops being a walk and starts needing equipment and judgement. Sources disagree on the distance in, from roughly six to eight miles, so do not plan a turnaround time off one figure. Useful mainly to parties who want a short summit morning on the glacier.

bivy.name: Three Fingers Lookout
bivy.water: None at the site — there is no potable water at the lookout and nothing to melt but snow.
bivy.capacity: Maximum occupancy of eight, first come first served. Accounts of the actual floor put it nearer three or four people plus two more on the sleeping platform, so eight is a squeeze rather than a plan. Arrive early or expect to be turned away by whoever got there first.
bivy.permit: No fee, no reservation and no permit — it is open to whoever reaches it first. There is no toilet: carry a waste bag and pack everything out, and do not put it in the Goat Flats toilet or leave it below the lookout. The volunteers who maintain the building ask that you take crampons off before going in, keep the shutters closed in bad weather and when you leave, leave nothing behind, and not force shutters that are locked.
bivy.notes: A 1930s fire lookout on the South Peak that climbers sleep in, reached by ladders with serious exposure — decide for yourself whether the final block is safe on the day. The door is never locked, but in winter and spring it can be frozen, swollen or buried, and the summit block itself is hard to climb then; summer is the season for it. Bring a tent as a fallback: it fills on good weekends and visitation is heavy even midweek. Sources disagree on whether there is usable ground to camp outside — some say pitch below the lookout, others say there is nowhere safe on the summit at all — so do not count on it. Published elevations for the lookout differ by several hundred feet, so none is recorded here.

bivy.name: Moose Creek bridge roadhead
bivy.water: Moose Creek at the bridge.
bivy.capacity: A roadside pull-in, not a designated site.
bivy.notes: The bridge on the Mine Road was closed and barricaded in 2008 and the ground beside it is where parties sleep in their vehicles. The route's own description recommends it, and the reason is the length of the day: twelve to fourteen hours car to summit means a start well before dawn, and this is the only way to get one without carrying a camp uphill.

bivy.name: Whitehorse Ridge platform above Lone Tree Pass
bivy.water: None running. There is a snow patch below Lone Tree Pass and nothing else until well past High Pass, so this camp is melt-only — fine in the April-to-June snow season the route is normally climbed, and dry once the patch has gone.
bivy.capacity: Room for a dozen or more tents on the broad crest — you will not be short of ground.
bivy.notes: The one large flat area on the entire route, about fifteen minutes of traversing beyond Lone Tree Pass, and by common consent where everyone camps; there is no ambiguity about where a party has pitched. Ground is usually snow, so expect to dig a platform. It is an exposed crest with a view from Baker to Dome Peak and nothing to hide behind. Watch the slope below the pass — parties have reported fresh rockfall and snow-roller debris appearing overnight. Published elevations for Lone Tree Pass itself differ, from about 4,800 to 5,000 ft.

bivy.name: Below High Pass at the first running water
bivy.water: The first running water on the route — the reason to come this far.
bivy.capacity: Not published.
bivy.notes: The mid-summer alternative, once the snow patch below Lone Tree Pass has melted and the ridge camp has no water at all. It costs another long traverse but puts you at the head of the basin, below the large talus field that is High Pass, with a short summit morning onto the Whitehorse Glacier. Note that High Pass is a feature of this route and not a separate approach.

bivy.name: Lower Depot Creek bench
bivy.water: Depot Creek, alongside.
bivy.capacity: Not published — informal ground rather than an established site.
bivy.permit: Inside North Cascades National Park, so an overnight needs a wilderness permit; cross-country camping is allowed only on durable surfaces and not in meadows or within 100 ft of water.
bivy.notes: Where the valley flattens and opens out above the Depot Creek Falls headwall. Parties use it two ways: as a shorter first day when the falls have taken longer than expected, and on the way out to put an hour of walking behind them. From here a scramble up and left onto the big buttress is a shortcut toward the Redoubt Glacier.

bivy.name: Ouzel Lake
bivy.water: The lake and Depot Creek at its outlet — glacier-fed and milky, and no source reports it failing. Some parties pitch a little above the outlet for easy access.
bivy.capacity: No published tent count; parties regularly find others already there. The number that actually binds is the permit cap of six people.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit, walk-up only — the cross-country zones covering this approach, Depot and Spickard, cannot be reserved in advance. Both cap a party at six people; Depot issues six permits a night and Spickard three. Ask at the Wilderness Information Center which of the two your intended site falls in, because published sources do not state the boundary. Camping is allowed only on durable ground and not within 100 ft of water. The approach begins in British Columbia and crosses the border on foot at the boundary monument, where there is a trail register; carry passports.
bivy.notes: The standard high camp and the one that serves both Spickard and Redoubt, on flat sandy treeless benches and a gravel moraine at the head of the valley below the calving front of the Redoubt Glacier. Six to nine hours and roughly 3,300 ft from the road, and the crux of getting here is the Depot Creek Falls headwall — over 900 ft of wet, slippery ground with a greasy rock step, where parties have found fixed hand lines at the two vertical sections. That headwall, not the distance, is why the lower bench gets used. Despite the route's name, the line turns off well before the pass that leads to Silver Lake and never reaches it; Silver Lake is a camp on the separate Silver Creek approach from Ross Lake.

bivy.name: Bedal Creek roadhead
bivy.water: Carry it, or take it from Bedal Creek on the way in.
bivy.capacity: Roadside parking, not a designated site.
bivy.permit: A Northwest Forest Pass is named as the required parking permit by most sources, though not all agree; carry one.
bivy.notes: Worth recording because it is the overnight most Sloan parties actually use. The Corkscrew from Bedal Creek is a reasonable single day of thirteen or fourteen hours for a fit party, and successful ascents in under twelve hours are common, so the usual pattern is to sleep at the trailhead and start around four in the morning rather than carry a camp to the ridge.

bivy.name: Bedal-Sloan saddle
bivy.water: A tarn at the saddle, and it is the weak point — it is stagnant, and parties have found frog and mosquito larvae in it. Better water is a short way above, around 5,500 ft, where small streams cascade down; fill there rather than at the pond.
bivy.capacity: Four to six tents, so leave room for another party.
bivy.notes: The first camp on the ridge, reached by traversing open and partly brushy slopes past a small lake. Usable, but the ridge above is the better camp and most parties who carry a camp go the extra distance. Elevation is given as either 5,330 or 5,380 ft depending on the source.

bivy.name: Ridge above the Sloan Glacier
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams below camp; the last running water is around 6,000 ft, and above that you are melting snow.
bivy.capacity: Several pleasant spots, with one dry site big enough for about four tents — more if you are willing to pitch on snow.
bivy.notes: The preferred high camp, on the crest overlooking the glacier with a long view. From here it is about half a mile of traverse east-southeast to the saddle near 5,900 ft and then up to gain the glacier around 6,800 ft, which makes for a short summit morning. Expect to camp on snow through June; the route's window is squeezed at both ends, with routefinding through the heather benches hard when they are still buried and the glacier growing impassable late in the season.

bivy.name: Tarn below Isolation Lake
bivy.water: The tarn, with a snowfield just above it feeding meltwater.
bivy.capacity: Not published.
bivy.permit: Core Enchantment Zone overnight permit — see the note on the Inspiration Lake entry; the same rules apply everywhere in the basin.
bivy.notes: A climbers' base camp rather than a scenic one: an unnamed tarn a tier below Isolation Lake, the first large lake reached coming over Aasgard Pass. Chosen for easy water, comparatively few insects and shelter below the open upper benches, at the cost of about two miles with a little climbing to reach the peak. Fires are prohibited here, as everywhere in the basin.

bivy.name: Inspiration and Perfection Lakes
bivy.water: The lakes.
bivy.capacity: No published tent count for any site in the basin. The permit is the real constraint: the Core Zone quota counts people entering per day rather than groups, and the whole of a permitted group must camp together at one site.
bivy.permit: An Enchantment Permit Area overnight permit is required from 15 May to 31 October, and Prusik's camps lie in the Core Enchantment Zone, which is allocated by lottery. Maximum group size is eight. Camp only on ground already worn bare — do not clear vegetation, move rocks or build walls. Fires are prohibited anywhere above 5,000 ft or within half a mile of a lake, which rules them out at every camp in this basin; solid-fuel and wood-burning stoves are also prohibited above 5,000 ft, but liquid and canister gas stoves are allowed. Dogs are not permitted anywhere in the Enchantment Permit Area, and no stock is allowed in the Core Zone. Maximum stay is fourteen consecutive days. Two traps worth knowing: a Snow Zone permit lets you climb here for the day but you must camp at or below Upper Snow Lake, and a Colchuck Zone permit does not allow camping above the 6,500 ft contour below Aasgard Pass. A Core Zone permit, by contrast, allows camping in any of the five zones on the way in or out.
bivy.notes: The most used camping ground in the basin, on the benches and the bluff between the two lakes, and the closest general camp to the peak — the signed path toward Prusik Pass leaves the western shore of Perfection Lake. Open granite and heather, thoroughly worn in, and shared with mountain goats that come in for salt. The exposed benches right at Isolation and Tranquil Lakes are above treeline and windy by comparison.

bivy.name: Squaw Lake
bivy.water: The lake.
bivy.capacity: Several sites around the shore.
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness, Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Cle Elum Ranger District: a wilderness permit and a trailhead parking pass. Stock parties are restricted to designated stock sites within half a mile of this lake, and those sites may not be used by a party without animals.
bivy.notes: The lower staging camp on the Cathedral Rock trail, about 1,500 ft above the Tucquala Meadows trailhead. It melts out noticeably earlier than Peggys Pond, which makes it the fallback in a heavy snow year or when the pond is full, at the cost of roughly two miles and 750 ft that you have to make up on summit day.

bivy.name: Peggys Pond
bivy.water: The pond, and a stream draining the east side of the mountain about a quarter mile northwest. No source reports either failing through the season.
bivy.capacity: Several larger sites right around the water and quieter ones further out; it is popular enough that on a busy evening the last free site takes finding. Early in July the constraint is snow rather than competition — parties have found the pond only part-thawed with just a few dry tent pads.
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness, Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Cle Elum Ranger District — a self-issue wilderness permit and a trailhead parking pass, with no quota or lottery. Campfires are prohibited above 5,000 ft on this side of the wilderness, which includes the pond, and building wind walls or fire rings is asked against. Several sites and paths here are signposted as closed for restoration and must not be used. There is a privy a quarter mile beyond the pond. Note that the wilderness order's 200 ft shoreline camping ban names five other lakes and does not apply here, so the setback some parties expect is not a rule at this pond — the marked restoration closures are.
bivy.notes: The standard base camp for the peak. The spur leaves the Cathedral Pass trail at the first switchback on the descent toward Deep Lake, signed as unsuitable for stock, which undersells it — the last mile carries sheer drop-offs, loose rock and steep user-built sections. Mosquitoes are the defining hazard rather than the terrain: reports in late July and early August describe them as ferocious, and it is the reason some parties camp higher.

bivy.name: East summit bivouac
bivy.water: Snowmelt only — this is a snow-season site.
bivy.capacity: One party. There is room for a small tent at best, and the party who used it slept out without one.
bivy.notes: A flat spot roughly 200 ft below the east summit, a little above the traverse toward the middle and west summits, reached by taking the Hyas Creek drainage and a snow couloir below the east peak. A deliberate choice rather than a forced night out — the party went past Peggys Pond specifically to escape the insects, and found none at that height. It only works while the drainage and couloir hold snow, so it is a spring and early-summer option; other parties have slept on the summit itself the same night.

bivy.name: Lower Lena Lake
bivy.water: The lake. There is no potable water at the trailhead, so this is the first fill.
bivy.capacity: Designated sites on both sides of the lake, first come and no reservation.
bivy.permit: Olympic National Forest. No overnight fee and no permit, but a Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is needed to park at the Lena Lake trailhead. Camp in the designated sites only; fourteen-day stay limit.
bivy.notes: Three miles in, and worth knowing about mainly so you do not mistake it for the climb's camp — it is a further three miles and about a thousand feet below the ground climbers actually use. It suits a party arriving late in the day or a first night split, not a summit bid.

bivy.name: Brothers base camp at Lena Forks
bivy.water: The East Fork of Lena Creek runs beside the flat spots, so filtering is easy and reliable. Do not be alarmed on the way in: lower down the valley the creek sinks into the boulders and runs underground, and the bed can be dry on the surface in late summer. That is normal and says nothing about the water at camp.
bivy.capacity: Four or five separate sites scattered through the trees. It does fill — parties have arrived to find every one taken and had to walk on to the next.
bivy.permit: Olympic National Forest, The Brothers Wilderness — and note this is national forest, not the national park, so there is no wilderness permit, reservation or quota, whatever some route pages say. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is required to park. Party size is capped at twelve, and caching gear for more than twenty-four hours is prohibited. Camp sits just below the wilderness fire line, which makes it the one place on this route where an open fire is legal.
bivy.notes: The base camp for the route, at the confluence of the forks of the East Fork of Lena Creek, roughly five to six miles in and about three miles beyond the north end of Lena Lake. Deep forest with little sun, and the ground is a lumpy mess of long-decayed fallen trees rather than flat duff. The trail beyond Lena Lake is unmaintained — blowdown, washouts and flagging tape — and parties routinely lose it, especially walking in at night. The reliable cue that you have gone past the forks is sound: the creek suddenly drops away and goes quiet. Snow lies at camp into spring. There is a fire ring, but one party found it burned over a foot down into the root mat, so think before lighting it.

bivy.name: Upper camp above the forks
bivy.water: Not published for the camp itself. The last water on the route is at or near treeline, around 4,000 ft; above that everything is carried, and parties fill two or more litres there for the summit and the return.
bivy.capacity: Not published.
bivy.permit: This camp is above the 3,500 ft wilderness fire line: stoves only, and gathering wood here is prohibited outright.
bivy.notes: A second camp area further up the basin, reached by following the cairned way trail toward the left fork until a small meadow opens. One trip record names it the East Lena Creek Basin and treats it as a separate place from the forks camp, and it is the only source for the elevation, so treat that figure as unconfirmed. It buys a little height at the cost of losing the legal fire and the known water.

bivy.name: Royal Creek
bivy.water: Royal Creek, immediately beside the sites.
bivy.capacity: Permitted for groups of up to twelve.
bivy.permit: Olympic National Park wilderness permit, required for every overnight stay year-round and reserved through Recreation.gov; you may only camp in the area named on your permit. Bear canisters are required in every wilderness camp in the park. This is the one Royal camp where campfires are allowed — it is the only division in the basin not designated no-fire, because it sits below the park's 3,500 ft campfire limit.
bivy.notes: Forested sites low in the valley, well short of the basin. An approach camp for a party arriving late rather than a base for the climb: the summit is a long way above, past Royal Lake and the upper basin.

bivy.name: Lower Royal Meadow
bivy.water: Royal Creek.
bivy.capacity: Permitted for groups of up to six.
bivy.permit: Olympic National Park wilderness permit, camp only in the area named on it, bear canisters required. No campfires.
bivy.notes: Subalpine sites beside the creek a short way below Royal Lake — a useful fallback when the lake itself is booked out, at the cost of a little height on summit day.

bivy.name: Royal Lake
bivy.water: Royal Lake and Royal Creek. Filter, boil or treat everything. No source reports either failing through the season.
bivy.capacity: Published counts disagree sharply — one account describes ten sites of which only two hold more than a single tent, another says the lake takes eight parties. What is certain is the permit: a group of six, with one separate group site for parties of seven to twelve.
bivy.permit: Olympic National Park wilderness permit, and this is a quota area — reserve on Recreation.gov, which opens in mid-April for the mid-May to mid-October season. There are no longer any self-issue paper permits at the trailhead. Camping in designated sites only, bear canisters required, and no campfires anywhere in Royal Basin. Parties of seven or more must use the designated group site at the lake; affiliated groups may not combine past twelve people and must camp at least a mile apart. The trail is closed to stock at the park boundary. There are composting toilets at the lake. Parking at the Upper Dungeness trailhead, which is national forest, needs a Northwest Forest Pass.
bivy.notes: The common base camp, about seven miles in, with a seasonal ranger camp up-valley. Reckon on roughly five hours from Shelter Rock to the summit — but note that published descriptions place Shelter Rock both above and below the lake, so work out which you are looking at before you time anything off it.

bivy.name: Upper Royal Basin
bivy.water: Tarns, creeks and snowmelt throughout the basin. Nothing published suggests any of it dries up.
bivy.capacity: No reliable current figure. An older account describes the basin taking around a dozen people in up to four groups, after a period of overuse led the park to tighten numbers — that is more than a decade old, so ask rather than assume.
bivy.permit: A park wilderness permit is still required, but this is not a designated-site camp: pitch on bare ground or gravel. Because Recreation.gov lists only the designated camps, an upper-basin or cross-country booking is made by telephoning the Wilderness Information Center instead. No campfires.
bivy.notes: The climbers' camp, a mile and about 500 ft above Royal Lake, and the point the standard route description measures the summit day from. A maze of tarns, moraines, heather, snowfields and house-sized boulders; the flattest ground is on the gravel bars beside the tarn. One account asks parties not to camp right at Imperial Tarn. Sources put the basin at 5,600 ft and its tarns nearer 5,700, so the figure here is approximate. Early July is the usual compromise on timing: the route wants snow still covering its loose rock, while the camps want to have melted out. Do not confuse this with Deception Basin, which appears in the same permit system but serves the alternative route on the far side of the peak.
